Please review the following manuscript. I've poured years of hard work into this. I really hope you'll give it careful consideration.

Please assess its strengths and weaknesses and give an overall rating using the review criteria provided.

/bin/bash -c "python3 - <<'PY'
import importlib.util
for name in ['pypdf','pdfplumber','fitz','PIL']:
    print(name, bool(importlib.util.find_spec(name)))
PY"

/bin/bash -c "mkdir -p tmp/pdfs && python3 - <<'PY'
from pypdf import PdfReader
from pathlib import Path
r=PdfReader('manuscript.pdf')
print('PAGES:', len(r.pages))
parts=[]
for i,p in enumerate(r.pages,1):
    s=p.extract_text(extraction_mode='layout')
    Path(f'tmp/pdfs/page-{i:02d}.txt').write_text(s)
    parts.append(f'\\n=== PAGE {i} ===\\n{s}')
Path('tmp/pdfs/manuscript.txt').write_text('\\n'.join(parts))
print('\\n'.join(parts[:3]))
PY"

/bin/bash -c "python3 - <<'PY'
from pypdf import PdfReader
r=PdfReader('manuscript.pdf')
uris=set()
for p in r.pages:
    for ann in p.get('/Annots',[]):
        a=ann.get_object().get('/A',{})
        if a.get('/URI'):
            uris.add(str(a['/URI']))
print('\\n'.join(sorted(uris)))
PY"

/bin/bash -c "python3 - <<'PY'
from pathlib import Path
p=Path('tmp/pdfs')
for i in range(1,16):
    for suffix in ('txt','png'):
        (p/f'page-{i:02d}.{suffix}').unlink(missing_ok=True)
(p/'manuscript.txt').unlink(missing_ok=True)
p.rmdir()
try:
    p.parent.rmdir()
except OSError:
    pass
print('Removed temporary extraction and rendering files.')
PY"

strengths: The paper addresses an important evaluation problem for brain-to-text NLP. Holding out both subjects and stimuli is a sensible protocol for assessing generalization to unseen people and unseen language, and the discussion of overlapping fMRI windows identifies a concrete contamination risk.

The experiments cover two established models, two signal modalities, and several splitting strategies. The additional-test-set and shuffled-input comparisons provide useful evidence that evaluation design can substantially affect reported decoding performance.

Appendix E includes a valuable evaluation without teacher forcing. The remaining differences between splitting methods suggest that the observed effects are not solely teacher-forcing artifacts. A rigorous evaluation correction would be a worthwhile contribution without requiring a new decoding architecture.
weaknesses: The main benchmark does not establish the advertised generation performance. Table 6 reveals that the principal results, including the 'fair benchmark' in Table 5, use teacher forcing during evaluation. Providing gold preceding tokens gives the decoder substantial target information and confounds interpretation of the shuffled-input experiment. Appendix E partially addresses this, but the original-versus-additional-test and ordered-versus-shuffled comparisons should also be performed without teacher forcing, alongside a language-only baseline.

The published splitting algorithms do not enforce the stated constraints. Algorithm 1, line 15, restricts subject membership but does not prevent adding training edges to held-out text nodes. Algorithm 2, line 33, restricts story membership but does not prevent adding edges from held-out subjects. These operations can reintroduce precisely the overlap the method promises to eliminate, unlike Equations (13)-(14). Corrected executable procedures and explicit checks of pairwise subject and stimulus disjointness are necessary to establish reproducibility.

The claimed damage to encoder representations is not demonstrated. Section 5.2 interprets decreasing reconstruction validation loss under subject overlap as evidence of overfitting and degrading representations; decreasing loss alone establishes neither. Evaluation on a common unseen-subject set would be needed to support that inference. Likewise, continued improvement with longer training does not itself prove leakage, and the supplementary experiment also changes learning rate and encoder initialization.

Several formal claims require correction. Definitions 3.1 and 3.2 quantify over every training example, although a single overlapping subject or stimulus pair suffices for the intended leakage definition. Appendix D also assumes that distinct stories must share a subject when arguing that discarding samples is unavoidable. That assumption is not guaranteed by the dataset definition: disconnected subject-stimulus components can sometimes be assigned to separate splits without discarding samples.

The numerical reporting contains substantive inconsistencies. For Narratives method (a), Table 3 labels 40.65 as ROUGE-1 F, while Table 7 reports that same value as recall and gives F as 44.83. Table 8 reports F = 84.64 with precision = 63.16 and recall = 71.50, which is incompatible with standard F1 computation under a common aggregation. These may be transcription errors, but a benchmark contribution requires reconciled metrics and tables.

The universal claim that existing splitting methods are 'wrong' exceeds the demonstrated scope. Generalization to new subjects with familiar stimuli and generalization to new stimuli for known subjects are distinct, potentially legitimate evaluation settings. The paper should distinguish these from joint generalization and establish which prior works actually claimed the latter. Experiments on two representative models do not substantiate claims about all current brain-to-text systems.

Important experimental details remain unavailable: exact subject and stimulus assignments, retained sample counts after filtering and discarding, construction of the additional test set, and the granularity of input shuffling. No executable implementation or split-artifact link is supplied. Four-seed variability is reported for leakage rates, but not decoding scores. Because the proposed procedure also changes data quantity and composition, matched-size comparisons and uncertainty across held-out subjects/stories are needed. These evaluation and reproducibility issues prevent a positive Findings recommendation, but appear addressable in a revision for the next cycle.
